routes.description: Establish physical resurrection as the best cumulative explanation of Jesus's death, the missing body or empty tomb, reported individual and group appearances, early bodily-resurrection proclamation, conversions, and costly witness conduct.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the principal historical data are sufficiently established, concern a physically risen Jesus, and are explained more adequately by resurrection than by visionary, literary-development, relocation, theft, or other rival accounts.

motionBridge.description: If Jesus died and afterward returned in the same transformed physical body, then Jesus physically rose from the dead and the motion's central conclusion is satisfied.

centralBridges.description: The sources must sufficiently establish the death, bodily-resurrection proclamation, appearances, and missing-body or empty-tomb data used in the cumulative inference.
Pauline and Gospel testimony must support bodily continuity between the crucified Jesus and the reported risen Jesus rather than merely disembodied survival or vision.
Resurrection must explain the established data with greater overall adequacy and fewer strained auxiliary assumptions than the principal non-resurrection alternatives.
Conversions, proclamation, and costly conduct must support sincere witness grounded closely enough in the alleged events to contribute to the resurrection inference.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Rival and later miracle reports must be assessed consistently, with relevant evidential differences determining whether they undermine or reinforce openness to the resurrection claim.
Roman practice, Pilate's political incentives, and the burial narratives must leave a known tomb and subsequent missing body historically plausible.

routes.description: Show that the surviving testimony does not historically warrant a physical resurrection because its key facts are uncertain, its appearance material may be visionary or developed, and relevant natural or literary alternatives remain viable.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the evidence fails to establish firsthand physical appearances and a securely known empty tomb, or if rival explanations account for the established data well enough that physical resurrection is not historically warranted.

motionBridge.description: If the available evidence does not warrant concluding that Jesus returned in a physical body after death, then the affirmative burden on the motion remains unmet.

centralBridges.description: Dating, dependence, authorship, narrative development, and lack of independent corroboration must materially limit what can be established about postmortem appearances and the tomb.
Appearance testimony must remain compatible with visionary experience or later physical elaboration rather than uniquely indicating encounters with a bodily risen Jesus.
Temporary burial, relocation, theft, or uncertainty about any empty tomb must remain sufficiently plausible alternatives to bodily resurrection.
Persecution, martyrdom, conversion, and movement growth must fail to connect securely enough to firsthand knowledge of a physical resurrection to establish that event.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Comparable Mormon and other religious testimony must expose whether the affirmative applies a consistent evidential standard to sincere, collective, costly, or persistent rival claims.
Narrative function, apologetic purpose, and inter-account tensions must provide viable explanations for features offered as marks of tomb-story authenticity.

sections.title: Historical method and source access
sections.rationale: This issue determines what Paul, the Gospels, Acts, and later testimony can establish given chronology, authorship, dependence, corroboration, and the evidential standard appropriate to the motion.

sections.title: Physicality and appearance testimony
sections.rationale: The motion specifically concerns physical resurrection, making the interpretation of individual and group appearances, Pauline bodily language, visions, and later narrative detail indispensable.

sections.title: Burial, empty tomb, and body disposition
sections.rationale: A known burial and missing body can support bodily resurrection, while uncertainty, temporary burial, relocation, theft, and narrative construction supply competing accounts of the same alleged data.

sections.title: Proclamation, conversion, and costly witness
sections.rationale: Early bodily-resurrection proclamation, conversions, apostolic conduct, persecution, and martyrdom matter only insofar as they connect sincere belief to informed access to the alleged event.

sections.title: Rival miracles and comparative standards
sections.rationale: Mormon, Marian, and other supernatural claims test whether collective testimony, persistence, suffering, incentives, and theological fit are being assessed by a consistent comparative standard.

sections.title: Cumulative explanatory inference
sections.rationale: The final burden requires comparing resurrection with visionary, literary, relocation, theft, and combined alternatives across all sufficiently established evidence rather than considering each datum in isolation.
